utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Margetts, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Witness KRAJ 682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then protective measures are face distortion, voice distortion, pseudonym, and private session for identifying portions of his evidence. Then I think for the witness to enter the courtroom we have to pull down the curtains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, it occurs so me while we're waiting there is a small matter. It might be useful just to use the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was that question of the -- the revised material in relation to those three exhumation experts. Your Honour, the position was we -- we received that in our locker, well, no earlier than Monday and -- and we think Monday. Your Honour, there shouldn't be very much difficulty if that were acceptable to the Trial Chamber and my dealing with it in the course of the next week. But, Your Honour, strong preference for not dealing with this week if that were acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we are close to the -- to the date where the Prosecution will close its case. But if we have a few of these loose ends which are mainly to be dealt with, I wouldn't say at an administrative level but at least to give decisions, it needs to further Court time. I take it we will hear the position of the Defence on it, and most likely we'll be able to give a decision without -- without any further oral arguments. So as such, it would not be a major problem, I would think. But, of course, I -- I'm hesitating between two things, first, to hurry up, and, second, to take your time during the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. We'll see about all that probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 682. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 682, we'll not call you by your own name. We'll use as a pseudonym 682. Your face cannot be seen by the outside world. Your own voice cannot be heard by the outside world. And whenever we'll deal with anything that could reveal your identity, we'd go into private session so that even the content of your testimony could not be heard. Witness 682, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness 682, please be seated. May I remind the parties to switch off their microphones when the witness speaks. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed. You'll -- Witness 682, you'll first be examined by Mr. Margetts, counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the pseudonym sheet could be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could the pseudonym sheet be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why not ask the witness whether his name and date of birth appear correctly on that without giving any further information. Does it appear correctly, Witness 682?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P916, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, on the 8th of April, 1992, did you receive information that you and your family should leave Zvornik city? And for reasons related to your protective measures, if you could just simply answer that question either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: No. But I left on the 8th of April and I moved my family out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, did you take your wife out of Zvornik city to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And having taken your wife to Serbia, did you then return to Zvornik city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. On that very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was Zvornik city taken over on the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: No. It was on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And on the 9th of April, 1992, did you and other members of your family and some Muslim neighbours leave and go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And on the 13th of April, 1992, did you return to your house in Zvornik city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you returned on the 13th of April, 1992, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I reported to the Crisis Staff and at that time I only performed guard duties outside in the streets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Where was the Crisis Staff located on the 13th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: In the Alhos factory in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you reported to the Alhos factory, who did you meet with first and what did they direct you to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: They told me that these guard duties should be organised. There weren't many inhabitants, so it was necessary for patrols to be organised in the area in which they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness. I asked you two questions in one there. Can you answer this question: When you went to the Alhos factory, who did you meet with first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I met the secretary, Stevo Radic, who told me that I should report to Zuco, which I did. He said that these guard duties were being organised in the neighbourhoods that we lived in and there weren't many inhabitants who had remained in Zvornik. They were of various ethnic groups, and it was necessary to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You described Stevo Radic as the secretary. Was he the secretary of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Even before the war he worked in the municipality. He was a secretary - that's what I said - because he issued those passes. You'd have to contact him for passes and for authority to move around the town and to move out of the town if you wanted to go to Yugoslavia. So he was involved in administrative matters and that is why I said that he was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And he informed you that you should report to Zuco. Is Zuco the nickname of a man by the name of Vojin Vuckovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you -- and you did, in fact, report to Zuco, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Where was Zuco located when you reported to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Zuco was on the first floor, the last door to the left. That's where he had an office and that's where people would go to see him. One had to pass by the duty officer to see him, and across -- opposite the office there was an office in which Stevo Radic performed his administrative duties. So I went there, reported to him, and he said that it was necessary to organise things to ensure that everything was orderly in the town. He said that he wanted to prevent accidents from occurring, as we inhabitants knew what the situation was. I went to see him. I said that there were Muslims in the neighbourhood, that there were very few Serbs there, so I and the Muslims went on patrol together. I was accompanied with another Muslim when we went on patrol. He said that it didn't matter if there was a Muslim who went on patrol too because he was living there at the time too. That's what he said at the time and that was, in fact, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And when you described the location of Zuco's office and Stevo Radic's office, those offices were located in the Alhos building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know the late Sejfudin Hadziefendic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. Sejfudin, he was a locksmith in Zvornik, a fairly prominent and respected man, and he was an honest man. Some people took him to the Crisis Staff together with his son. At the time, I was leaving - I don't know what the date was; I was leaving the Crisis Staff at the time - it was around 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening. Night was already falling. I couldn't see who was in the car. They asked me whether I knew who the person in the car was and I said, "No, I don't know him. I can't recognise him if I can't see him." When I saw him, I greeted Sejfudin. And as I said he was a very honest man. And that's what I said. I said they shouldn't take him away, they should apologise to him. After the war when Sejfudin came to see me, he said that they took him home and apologised to him. I don't know what happened to him after that, though, nor do I know what happened after he left Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did that meeting with Sejfudin Hadziefendic occur in April 1992 after you'd reported to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. It was between the 14th and the 22nd. It was during that eight- to ten-day period. But I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know why Sejfudin was being brought to the Crisis Staff when you met him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did Biljana Plavsic visit Zvornik in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I know that she visited the place on one occasion. She was accompanied by Princess Karadjordjevic at the time, because as far as I know, she was -- Mrs. Plavsic was a royalist and so she liked to associate with such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When she visited Zvornik, did she attend the Alhos factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: She went to the Alhos factory. I was in another department at the time. When they closed the door, they said we couldn't go out into the corridor because Biljana Plavsic was coming. And that's why I know that she came. But I did not see her on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were you informed who she met with when she visited the Alhos factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic was there. There were some others who came to the meeting too. Probably Mr. Brano Grujic as well. I don't know what they discussed because it was all done behind closed doors. So I really don't know who was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And -- and just to be clear, was this in mid to late April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I think it was in mid April, before the 27th, before they went to Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In early May 1992, did the Crisis Staff move from the Alhos building in Karakaj to the post office building in the centre of Zvornik city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: It moved across the road from the post office, which is where the Ministry of the Defence and the TO Staff had been before the war. It moved to that building at the beginning of May or the end of April. I can't remember the exact date, but when I reported to the Crisis Staff, to the TO Staff, well, I reported to them at the beginning of May and they moved a few days -- they had already moved. That was a few days after Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who Aco Sekanic is and the position he occupied from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Aco Sekanic. That's his name. He was in the TO Staff and at the time I think he was the assistant commander or something like that, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When the Zvornik Brigade was formed, was he the duty officer for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: When the brigade was formed, the duty officers would change every 24 hours. And there was also a junior duty officer. And these two officers would change in the course of 24 hours. So he was there and he was on duty occasionally. That depended on the schedule. So there were others who also had such a position, other officers in the brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On or around 4 May 1992, did you meet Aco Sekanic in town and did he direct you to report to Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. He told me to report to the staff, to report to the commander in order to be assigned duties and in order to act in accordance with my establishment. I said that that wasn't a problem; I'd no longer be on guard duty; I should report there. And I reported there that evening, as he said I should do, and the commander then told me that I should turn up in uniform if I had a uniform. And if I didn't have a uniform that I would receive one. He said, "Come in the morning and you will be assigned your duties." That's what I did. I reported in the morning. They told me to come at 7.00 in the morning. They weren't there because they were involved in some sort of combat task. Later on I found out they went towards Satnija and to Nezuk. I spent the entire day waiting for them. Up until 6.00 I was on assigned duty. They said "Turn up in the morning," and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could just stop you there before you explain any further. I'll just have a couple of clarifying questions and then we may go into private session. It's also just indicated to me that you're being simultaneously translated and it's -- it would be helpful to the translators if you could just slow down the speed of your speech. So just one question. You referred to the commander. When you referred to the commander, were you referring to Marko Pavlovic, who at that time was the commander of the TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I'd like to refer to witness now to the document that is at tab 1 of the presentation binder, and if that document could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, can you have a look at that map that's been presented to you and can you confirm that both the Novi Standard factory and the Alhos factory are correctly labeled and that is their locations represented there in the Karakaj industrial area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I can confirm that. It is correctly indicated on the map where Novi Standard and Alhos factories are. Because all the other companies located in the area are correctly marked, Glinica, Spaglum [phoen], plywood factory, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, just -- we are early in the testimony now. If these factories would have been located 300 metres to the north or 200 metres to the west, would that have changed anything? I mean, the witness says where they gathered. From his statement, at least, I do not find that -- the exact location and the positions, one to another, are of any great relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Contained within this witness's testimony there -- there is no argument the Prosecution would like to make. However, there could be some submission that the Prosecution will make in relation to the position of the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, I do not know what's -- what's going to be there. But exact locations without follow-up somewhere and giving it a greater weight than it seems to have at this moment would not assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just at this moment I'd just like to indicate that there -- this map has appeared before the Trial Chamber before, and I think it -- from memory, it was Exhibit P677, where the actual location was of some significance. And later we may be relating this Exhibit P918 to that previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it must have been another map because it's now been assigned. We saw a map of Zvornik. And let's not spend too much time. I -- I just want to invite you not to go in details which do not add anything to the core of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just observe I'm recorded on the transcript at line 7 as having said "yes." Now, I do occasionally say yes but I was going through one of my very quiet spells there, Your Honour, and actually said nothing at all for quite a few minutes. So I don't know how that rogue affirmative has crept in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You made it up now by these remarks, Mr. Stewart. I take it three lines for saying that you didn't say yes. Please proceed Mr. -- it's correct that it's a rogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. With a fourth line, Your Honour, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could return to map to the court usher. I'd now like to ask you a few questions about Mr. Marko Pavlovic, the TO Staff commander. Is Marko Pavlovic the real name of the gentleman who was the commander of the Territorial Defence, or was this an alias?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: At that time, we all knew him as Marko Pavlovic; however, I learnt later that his real name was Branislav Popovic. They said it was his real name, but I think that even that is not his real name because many people appeared under various aliases. They did not tell their real name. Others were called by nickname. With this person, it was the case that everybody addressed him as Marko Pavlovic without really knowing what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When was Marko Pavlovic appointed commander of the Territorial Defence? And for how long did he continue to occupy this position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: He was appointed on the 27th of April in the afternoon or in the evening, after their return from Kula. A meeting was held where he was appointed commander of the TO. That was on the 27th of April. And he remained commander all the way up to August, regardless of the fact that the brigade was set up sometime in the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm now going to refer to a series of documents that refer to Marko Pavlovic, and if the witness could be shown the document that appears at tab 2 in the presentation binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I direct the witness's attention to, first of all, the listing at paragraph 3. And just for reference, this -- this document already has an exhibit number. It's Exhibit P664. I direct the witness's attention first to paragraph 3. And there's the name that appears at item 2, and that's Stevo Radic. Is that the Stevo Radic that we previously referred to in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I also refer you to paragraph 4 and to the listing at paragraph -- at point 2, item 2, and that is Marko Pavlovic. Is that the Marko Pavlovic that we previously referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown the document which is at number -- tab 5. And this document already has the exhibit number P865A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, I'll first -- this is a document which is dated the 30th of May, 1992 and it's from the commander of the East Bosnia Corps Nikola Dencic, and it's directed to the Zvornik Territorial Defence headquarters. I'll first refer you to paragraph 3, and there's a reference in there to someone referred to as Major Marko - Branko Popovic. In light to have answer you've previously given in respect of Marko Pavlovic's use of an alias, is this a reference to the TO Staff commander Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. There is a reference to him. I told you I didn't know he was appointed liaison officer but he was in the same place, on the same job, at the same time when the Zvornik Brigade was established and he performed the same duties as when he was commander of the TO and the TO headquarters was across the street from the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are you able to explain this to the Court: The document here states that "The Zvornik Territorial Defence headquarters is to be transformed into the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade." But as I understand it, what in fact occurred was that there was the continued operation of the Zvornik Territorial Defence Staff and command headquarters and it operated alongside the command of the Zvornik Brigade. Is -- is that what your -- is that what you've told the Court this morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. They worked on parallel tracks. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have that answer redacted from the transcript. Sorry, I don't mean redacted. I mean if that could not be available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar is instructed to make the necessary redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What's -- the whole answer is being redacted or -- or what? I'm not absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, possibly if we could go into private session I could assist in an explanation of why it's necessary to redact that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, you referred to the fact that the TO Staff and the Zvornik Brigade command worked along parallel tracks. Was it possible for the Zvornik Brigade commanders and also for Marko Pavlovic, as the TO Staff commander, to issue orders to the military units in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd now like to refer to the document at tab 6. If that could be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is a certificate which has been issued by the commander Lieutenant Colonel Slobodan Vasilic. It's dated the 22nd of August, 1992, and it confirms the engagement of Marko Pavlovic in the Serbian army. First of all, who was Colonel Slobodan Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Colonel Slobodan Vasilic was the second commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, because the first one to be appointed was Vidoje Blagojevic. Vasilic was the second one to be appointed and he's writing a certificate here stating that the person in question is engaged in the Serbian army, but I wish to note that this is the date when he actually left. From -- left Zvornik, left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, you've explained clearly the fact that the TO Staff command and the Zvornik Brigade command were able -- both able to issue orders to the units in the area and that they worked on parallel tracks. Looking at that certificate, can you explain why it is that it's confirmed that Marko Pavlovic was in the Serbian army, and -- and is that consistent or inconsistent with your understanding of his status?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Every certificate of this kind that was issued was meant to justify absence from one's workplace. It meant that a person cannot be dismissed, let go, when they have such a certificate. Their work, their job had to wait for them. That is why such a certificate was issued to every soldier and every officer, to confirm that they are engaged in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know where Marko Pavlovic worked before he came to Zvornik and what his background was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: From what I learned after he left, he used to work in Vrbas or Sombor, in the oil-processing industry. But after he left Zvornik, I never met him again. So I don't know where he is now and what he came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was involved with any intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Well, when we were in detention in Bijeljina, he was brought too subsequently and he told the policeman that he was a warrant officer by rank and he told them his real name. That's how we found out his real name. Until then, we didn't know who he really was or what his job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I specifically mentioned whether or not he was in the intelligence service. You referred to the fact that he was a warrant officer by rank. Do you know what unit or -- or what division of the army he was engaged in, and which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: He was an intelligence officer, maybe of the former Yugoslavia, but he was either an intelligence or a counter-intelligence officer. But he was what we used to know as a civilian employee of the intelligence service. It is certain that he could not have had the rank of warrant officer if he had only worked in the FRY. He had to have been engaged earlier while the SFRY was still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, as I say, I don't wish to belabour this point, but when we referred to that certificate which is still before you - and it's Exhibit P919 from tab 6 - there's a reference to his engagement with the Serbian army. And you've clearly said that the TO Staff and the Zvornik Brigade command worked parallel. Both could order the units in Zvornik. This certificate indicates some formal engagement of Marko Pavlovic with the Serbian army. Is that consistent with your understanding or is that inconsistent with your understanding? Was he or was he not formally engaged with the Serbian army? And if he wasn't, then what was his relationship to the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, but I'll try to answer. He was engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska and the TO Staff, and I think that throughout the time he cooperated with both and came to briefings and contacted commanders. But what the exact relationship was, I don't know. All I know is that both issued orders. Again, I'm saying that I am not sure I understood your question correctly. I hope I gave you a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, that -- that was the topic that I was looking for further information on, and so I thank you for that answer. Earlier in your evidence you referred to the fact that you left Zvornik on the 9th of April and you took two Muslim neighbours with you into Serbia. Did Marko Pavlovic visit the house where these Muslim neighbours were in Serbia and did he make contact with these Muslims for any reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: One of those Muslims used to work in the Ministry of the Interior, that is, in the police. And when he heard on the radio that all employees of the police and various other services should report to work to perform their wartime assignments, he went to Zvornik to the Crisis Staff, where he saw Marko Pavlovic first, because he had to report to him, and since he is a native of Kula and has family there, this Muslim man really went to see him and talk to him about negotiating the release of some people who had been detained on the road between Divic and Drinjaca. At the moment of the conversation, they were in detention. So he talked to Marko Pavlovic. Marko Pavlovic took him to the house where these people were kept. And on that occasion, he also saw my father, and those two men stayed actually in my father's house. And even the wife of one of those men who had telephoned was also in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise an issue on the transcript of the translation. Mr. Karganovic informs me that a more apt translation of what the witness actually said in Serbian would have been that they issued orders to each other. I make no comment at all on the content, but -- but that's what Mr. Karganovic tells me about what was actually said in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could seek clarification from the witness possibly on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the interpreters would have any comment, because we highly appreciate the assistance of Mr. Karganovic but, of course, finally it's the interpreters who have the final word. But let's first seek clarification with the witness. And if there remains anything unclear, then we could ask the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, I must apologise to you for a second time about this matter relating to the command authority of Marko Pavlovic in that Territorial Defence Staff and the command authority of the Zvornik Brigade commanders. Learned counsel for the Defence has noted that possibly there was an interpretation error in one of the answers you previously gave, and that was this -- and so I'll ask you a question directed to this issue, and that is: Is it the case that the -- that Marko Pavlovic could issue orders to the command of the Zvornik Brigade and also could the command of the Zvornik Brigade issue orders to Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: My answer was this: Both of them issued orders to the subordinates and what their mutual relationship was, whether one issued orders to the other, that I don't know, but they both issued orders to us soldiers about what to do. Whether Marko Pavlovic issued orders to Vidoje Blagojevic or vice versa is something I don't know. They had their own internal briefings and arrangements and whether they had some distribution of work amongst themselves, I cannot tell you because I didn't attend their meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That fully clarifies the -- the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I suggest fewer comment from Mr. Margetts this morning following answers from the witness would be appreciated. It's been a number of comment this is morning. I know it's easy for them to slip out from counsel, but we would prefer that they didn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my defence I'd say the first comment was elicited by a question from the witness as to whether or not his answer fully answered my question. The second one, perhaps my friend has a -- has a point, and I will desist, unless specifically questioned by the witness for some confirmation in relation to his answer. Your Honour, if we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's confirmed on my screen, Mr. Margetts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Prior to the formation of the Zvornik Brigade, that is, during the course of April and May 1992, under whose command was Zuco and his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: At the time, since there was the TO Staff, it was under the TO Staff during that period of time, until the brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Once the brigade was formed, under whose command was Zuco and his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Under the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, because Zuco went to briefings and to give reports to the brigade command and also when it was necessary to obtain equipment and logistics, in order to obtain weapons and ammunition. So he would also come to the warehouse in the Standard building for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, if I could refer you to the document at tab 8, and that is already allotted the exhibit number P822, tab 41. This is a list of manpower and it's dated the 1st of May, 1992. utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: It says: "Authorised by the TO Staff commander." It's a list of units that were under Zuco's command. There's Vuckovic Dusko, Jorica Neskovic, and Dusko Stevan. And then it says that Jago Stevan was there from the 14th of May to the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'm just interested in whether or not you can make out the name that appears on the third line of the handwriting. Can you read that -- that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Nebojsa Nozica, and Vuckovic, Dusko, who is under number 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness, I'm not expressing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: And here it says "Stevo Radic." It says that the list was provided to him. Stevo Radic was the secretary in the municipality. It's a list of soldiers who were supposed to receive their salaries, and Stevo Radic is mentioned. He was provided with this and he received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was Stevo Radic responsible for distributing these payments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: All lists were provided to Stevo Radic, all lists of all units, so that he could calculate the amount of money each individual should be allocated as a salary. So he was provided with these lists. And then he was also provided with information on sanitary items, soap, washing powder, et cetera, for units. He was provided with such lists, which he could then authorise so that this -- these goods could be taken from some companies. Stevo Radic had the authority to issue items for personal hygiene and perhaps certain tins of food, mineral water, et cetera. So as the secretary, he had the authority to issue such items.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you for -- for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could now refer to tab 9, and if that could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P921.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, at -- at tab 9, we have a listing for payment for soldiers. The name Vojan Vuckovic, Zuco, appears at 41; the name Dusan Vuckovic appears at 44. utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: It's the signature -- the handwriting of Marko Pavlovic, TO Staff commander. Since there is no word "for" or "on behalf of" before the signature, that means that he signed this personally and I know this signature because he signed my laissez-passer when I had to go to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, we referred earlier to Stojan Pivarski. Did you ever have a conversation with Stojan Pivarski where he raised the issue of helping Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I talked to him sometime in early June or maybe mid-June, when he went to the staff and I was going to the staff too, to have lunch or something. So we went together. I set off from the depot and he was on his way there, too. So we ran into each other, and since we knew each other well, he told me, (redacted) (redacted) And he says, "I got a report, but I don't believe it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, please. Sorry, I believe there was a reference to a word that should be redacted. It wasn't translated in the English translation but I believe it's an identifying word, and it appears -- it appears at line 9. Page 40, line 9. If that could be redacted.

utterances.text: And I suggest that if you have similar questions, that we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P922.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, this is a information report from the Zvornik Brigade command, and there's a request for information so that payroll accounts can be prepared and payment of compensation for the month of June can be effected. The part of the document that I'd like you to refer to is the handwriting again, at the bottom of the document, and the heading there is submitted on the 18th of June, 1992 and the first three lines refer to the 1st Battalion, 2nd Battalion, and 3rd Battalion. If you could cast your eye to the right-hand side of this handwriting, you'll see that there are three names set out there: Niski, Pivarski, and Zuco. And in regard to Zuco, there is an arrow pointing from his name up toward the name of Niski. Was it your understanding that Zuco and his unit in June 1992 were part of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Zuco's Unit was at the time part of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, because he was on their lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If I could now refer to tab 11, which is P822, tab 39. utterances.text: 1st Battalion, because it says who belongs to which unit and it means that Zuco's Unit belonged to the 1st Unit. They didn't write "Igor Markovic" because that would have been longer; they just wrote "Zuco Group, 1st Battalion." That means the unit was under the command of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, if we could now move to the next document, which is at the -- tab 12. And there's a heading above the name Stojan Pivarski. Could you read that and inform the Court as to what that heading means, which reads: "Grupa Pivarskog 2nd Battalion." What does that heading mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: This is a unit under Pivarski's command. That is why it's written "Pivarski's Group under the command of the 2nd Battalion." You can see here where it says "Pivarski" in the third column it says "group commander." In short shrift, that means that this unit is under his command and then follows a list of the entire unit which was under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd now like to ask you a few questions about the gentleman that was listed in the document we saw at tab 10; that was Exhibit P922. And that's the gentleman by the nickname Niski. Do you know what his full name is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I think his name was -- his first name was Miroslav. I can't tell you his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But did you at one stage know what his full name was and is it the case that you just can't recall it at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I did. I did know his full name. I just can't recall it at the moment, because it's been 13 or 14 years. I can only remember "Miroslav," because even when I was talking to him, I never called him by last name; I just called him "Niski" or "Miroslav."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the leave of the Court, if I could refer the witness to tab 32 wherein a statement is provided by person of the nickname Niski. And if I could refer the witness to that statement just for the purpose of reading the name next to that nickname and confirming whether or not that refreshes his memory in an accurate description of the gentleman known as Niski's name. And for the record, tab 32 is P529 tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really -- I really don't have any problem with this. It's on this particular point. It's plain that this document speaks for itself on that smallish point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and thank you, learned counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, having looked at that document, can you confirm that Niski's name was Svetozar Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Right. Yes. And he got his nickname on the basis of the fact that he came from Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you could put that statement away. We won't refer again to that statement. When did you first meet Niski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I first met him sometime around the 25th or the 26th of April, before departing for Kula. I didn't have much contact with him on that occasion, but that's the first time I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Prior to your meeting him, did you know whether or not he had previously been in Zvornik? And if he had been, for what purpose was he in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Before that, I didn't know he had been coming to Zvornik. I learned only later that he had been in Zvornik and had been involved in the fighting in Zvornik, after which he left and then returned. I learned that from talking to Zuco, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When he was involved in the fighting in Zvornik, that is, prior to your meeting him, which unit was he fighting with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: In the Serbian volunteers guard, under the command of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When he returned to Zvornik on the 26th of April, under whose command was he from that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: At the outset, he was under the command of Zuco. He reported to him, at first, and then he received orders later on from Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to the Birac Brigade and ask you a few questions in relation to this brigade. First of all, who was Svetozar Andric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Svetozar Andric was the commander of the Bircani Brigade, whose command was in Sekovici, and his deputy was Bogunovic. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you see Svetozar Andric and Major Bogunovic in Zvornik during the period April 1992 through to the period July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I would see go Bogunovic from time to time in April in Zvornik. I was aware that Andric would come and go. I met him once without knowing that he's the commander. And I also saw Bogunovic a couple of times when we were together in the unit, when we were close to Caparde and when we would have -- when he would give some combat orders to Zuco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, Witness, we've previously discussed the relationship that Zuco had with the Zvornik Brigade. And by the nature of your last answer, you've indicated that also the deputy commander of the Birac Brigade would issue orders to Zuco. Are you able to inform the Court of what the relationship was between the Birac Brigade and the Zvornik Brigade? And just as a -- a matter of background, the Court is aware that they were both brigades within the East Bosnia Corps and they both had their area of operations. But can you explain to the Court how it was that a commander of the Birac Brigade would be giving orders to a unit such as Zuco's.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: He was able to issue orders to Zuco's unit because we, from the Zvornik Brigade, were attached, seconded to fill in a gap in the front line so that Zuco's Unit was closer to the Sekovici Brigade than to the Zvornik Brigade. They had radio communications with them, but they issued orders to us because we were closer. And once we are closer to their command, they would give us orders on a particular combat activity, because we filled a part of this front line, defence line, facing Sekovici, branching off towards Sapna and towards the Sekovici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could now refer to witness to tab 14, and if this document could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. It says "Sekanic A.," meaning Aleksandar Sekanic. He took over duty at 1800 hours. This worked in shifts and the duty operations officer was the one who received information on the latest developments on front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was the operations officer and the command of the Zvornik Brigade stationed at Novi Standard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes. He was stationed in Novi Standard on the first floor, and all incoming information either through communications or otherwise found its way to the duty service logbook. And somebody came in with the

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: what his unit was doing. Everybody who was coming in would report what was going on, on the front lines, either orally or through communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, again, if we could redact that portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, Witness, could you please carefully listen to the question and, to start with, limit your answer to what is specifically asked. utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the redaction is at 48, line 22. If that entire line could be struck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: and the offending portion precedes that.

utterances.text: Yes. By reading that line, Mr. Margetts, you caused that -- also your remarks in this respect have to be redacted. Yes? Please keep that in mind. Madam Registrar is instructed to ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have just one line different between your line and my line. When it is line 22 at your side, it's line 23 on my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Could I refer you to the entry that's on the page marked the last four digits 6516 and refers to contact that was made at 5.30 a.m. Presumably that would then be on the 29th of June. utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes, it is consistent, because everybody who would go to the command from units for whatever reason could take a message, because we had no direct lines, either telephone or radio lines, with the command, so that anybody going there on whatever errand could take a message personally so that people would know what to do next.

utterances.text: He would come to report -- everybody would come in to report around 8.00 a.m. about the situation on the front line and receive orders from the command. utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, again, we will need to redact that. If you could refrain unless specifically asked from describing your particular duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, you've described the fact that Zuco and all the other commanders of battalions and independent units would attend these morning briefings. Apart from attending the morning briefings, did Zuco attend the command on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Zuco would sometimes come on other occasions if he needed something urgently; although, generally speaking, he didn't come to the command that often, because he would be usually on the front line or somewhere else. But he would come in whenever he needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You mentioned that he didn't come there that often. Can you indicate to the Court how frequently he -- he would be at Novi Standard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Well, I can say that he would come once a day or maybe once in two or three days, depending on the developments on the front line. That dictated the frequency of his visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could now refer to the documents that are at tabs 15 and 16, and if both of those documents could be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The tab 15 would be P924. Tab 16 will be P925.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, the document that you find at P -- at that tab 15, which is marked P924, is a direction from the commander, Colonel Dragutin Ilic of the East Bosnia Corps to the command of all units, and he is indicating that an analysis of combat operations taken -- undertaken in the last 30 days, "will take place on the 13th of July, 1992." And this document's dated 6 July 1992. You'll note that one of the core issues that's noted is the issue set out at paragraph 2, item 6, and it's -- refers to "joint operations with volunteers and method of use." Now, this document, in fact, further useful information relating to what was intended there can be gleaned from the next document, so I'll refer, Witness, immediately, if you could refer to tab 16. And at tab 16, which is the next one along -- Witness, do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: No, I haven't got it before me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is a document apparently prepared in response to the order of Dragutin Ilic and it's prepared by the Birac Brigade. And the you look at the item on the second page of the English, item number 6, and on the -- the bottom item on the second page of the Serbian, and that item is headed "Experience with use of volunteers, ways of putting them to use." And I'll read what it says into the record. It says: "Three groups of volunteers who agreed to fight under joint command are currently in the zone of responsibility of the brigade. Those are mostly men with combat experience from Croatia. They were used to take -- to -- takeover of certain heights and combat in inhabited places." Witness, is that consistent with your experience of the use that units such as Zuco's and Pivarski's were put to by the Birac or the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes, it is consistent with such use, because whenever the threats were higher, they sent soldiers who were experienced to deal with such situations. Whenever this was required, that was the case. There were -- it says "three groups" here and then they were all together and later they had their commands in three different battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you a question about your arrest, and then I'm going to go into private session to describe further matters, but I -- I'd just like to -- and I will go into the details of your actual arrest and what took place and who arrested you, but if you could refrain from indicating those matters in open session. And if I could just ask you to describe how you and the other people who were arrested in August -- early August of 1992 and who were detained at the Bijeljina SJB, how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: The conditions were very difficult. There were 50 people who were held in a very small area. They had to strip to their underclothes. We had to urinate into pots, and one had to wait for several hours to go and defecate. When we were arrested, we were beaten. People's teeth were broken. Their ribs were broken. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's confirmed on my screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, you just described the fact that Momcilo Mandic drove through the checkpoint. He had a number of vehicles with him. When he returned and passed again through the checkpoint, some of those vehicles did not return. Witness, those vehicles that were with him, were they new vehicles that were not registered and were they consistent with the type of vehicle that was stored at the TAS factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Those vehicles were from the TAS factory. They were licenced. They had licence numbers and they had papers, but the papers were not in order. For instance, a vehicle claimed to have been manufactured in 1990 had papers dating back to an earlier year. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, did -- at some stage did Velibor Ostojic attempt to pass through the checkpoint? And do you know what occurred to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I hope that we do not go again into vehicles with -- I mean, this is not a case about stolen vehicles. This is a case about other things, as far as I understand. And so therefore it's not -- not clear to me what the relevance of this is, unless you would find it important to establish that there was an atmosphere where not everyone avoided to get the best out of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no intention of introducing this evidence with a purpose of demonstrating that point. If the witness could remove his headphones just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you take your headphones off, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the detention of the paramilitary unit was a matter that previous evidence we've introduced to the Chamber establishes was something referred to by the leaders of the Bosnian Serb state, and they indicated that the detention was for a specific reason and, in fact, this witness is the best witness to provide evidence of the real reason for that detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, you would say that they were blamed for thefts of cars committed by others? Is that ...? Or at least appropriation in a not regular way? Is ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order for us to -- to present material to the Court from which the Court can make a conclusion as to why they were detained, we need to, in our submission, present what -- what preceded their detention and a conclusion as to the reason for their detention may become expressed or at least be inferred from -- from those events that preceded the detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be more express. If learned Defence counsel has any objection to me putting this submission at this stage, the witness cannot hear it. The fact of the matter is this: That there was representations at the leadership level that the detention of the paramilitaries was in order to comply with their international regulations -- obligations or international humanitarian law obligations of prevention and punishment and there was an attempt to blame these paramilitaries for crimes that the internationals were alleging were committed by Bosnian Serb forces. We need to present the background matters, such as the discussion with the -- with the Presidency member Biljana Plavsic and the -- the substance of that discussion and the contact that these individuals had with the Minister of Justice and Minister of Information to demonstrate -- and also the -- the substance of the indictment that was levelled against them, which specifically referred to conduct at checkpoints, to provide the Court with the opportunity to understand the real reason for why they were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand from these papers and from the earlier answers that the witness, that they were -- I think you call it the scapegoat in English for what others might have done. But the main issue is that we are talking about cars. The core of this case is not cars and it becomes clear from the documents you have presented until now that at least they were not detained because they had ill-treated, beaten, killed, whatever, but that it was just in terms of cars worth more than a certain amount of money. Therefore, I really wonder whether we have to go into such details, because if you'd say -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's not about the type of behaviour which in the core of this case and whether they were then detained as scapegoats to cover up someone else's misbehaviour in terms of -- of theft or cars or whether it was anything else. The most important thing is, I take it, that it was -- that at least on paper it's cars. Whether they've stolen it, whether someone else has stolen it -- and it's not what is in the core of this case, and that is persecution of a certain population. Because one would not even know to whom these cars belonged or would we? Perhaps they --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I reassure you, and perhaps I should have done this earlier, I do not intend to ask any more questions about cars. The one thing I did want to deal with was an incident that occurred at the checkpoint with the Minister of Information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yes, but let's see. You are now aware of the concern of the Chamber. We are close to the finish of the second portion of this morning, where you said you might finish your examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can seek some guidance. When are we going to complete this session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I thoughts usually we do that -- we had a late start this morning, half an hour later than usual. Therefore, all the breaks are a bit later. We're now close to where we would have taken half an hour ago a break if we would have started at a normal time. So therefore when I was thinking about taking a break, I thought, No, let's give an opportunity to Mr. Margetts to finish his examination-in-chief. Yes, the witness has his earphones on again. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to require a little bit of -- a little bit further -- probably about 15 minutes at least to complete examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would finish within 10 minutes from now on, then we would stay within the -- stay within the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, what occurred to Velibor Ostojic at the Karakaj checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic was stopped in order to perform a check. He didn't want to stop because every combat unit has their own weapons as envisaged by establishment. Anyway, he was forced to get out of the car and he said to them, "You cannot act this way. Do you know who I am?" And the people from the checkpoint told them, "Everyone is equal in our eyes. They all have to show their IDs." And he replied, "I am the Minister of Information." And the man from the checkpoint told him, "Even if you were my own father, you would still have to show me your ID." So he was forced out of the car and made to lie down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you concentrate on the main points. Not too many details. Please proceed. What happened? He went out of the car. What was the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, that's -- that's an adequate answer. If I could move you on now and we could refer to tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if that could be given an exhibit number and presented under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P930, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And accordingly, if we could now move into private session and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And have a redaction made on from where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The introduction of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And are we now in private session, Your Honour? Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's reasonable just to repeat that fairly short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, when you were arrested and taken into custody in Bijeljina, you were interrogated, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: By just one person during your custody or by more than one person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: There were two persons. One interrogated and another one was present. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On -- were you interrogated on just one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: There were two interrogations. The first one was an interrogation where an inspector hit me. I asked him not to hit me and if he wanted to hear the truth, I was prepared to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't -- well, I'm -- I'm assuming that answer doesn't create a problem as far as the open and private session is concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not as far as I can see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't think it did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The -- I hadn't asked you about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, apologies. In fact, it does create a problem, and I would ask for a redaction of lines 6 to 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You take sequence of places? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: From the words (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's take that three lines out. And, Madam Registrar, you are instructed to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll -- I'll leave that second location till tomorrow, then, Your Honour. That would simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So far as Bijeljina was concerned, Witness, do you remember the names of anybody who was involved -- well, involved with those who arrested you, had you in custody, or interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I remember those people who conducted the arrest, who led the arrest. There was Mandic and Milenko Karisik. They led the operation of our arrest; the entire operation, that is. Whereas, in Bijeljina, if I remember the last name correctly, I was interrogated by an inspector named Govedarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, have you in the last three weeks or so been following any of the proceedings in this trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I don't follow any proceedings of the Tribunal, not only these proceedings. It's because of the schedule. When there are proceedings here, I am at work and I cannot follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Have you heard anything or had any discussion before you came to The Hague over the last two or three weeks about any of the proceedings in this trial? I should accept from that any -- any arrangements you've been making with anybody in The Hague. If I can leave that on one side. But any discussion with anybody out in your own country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I haven't discussed these proceedings with anyone at all, with the exception of my family, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Does the name Milorad Davidovic mean anything to you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Well, all I know is that he was also someone who acted as a commander of the police unit from Bijeljina. That's all his name means to me, and he was also in charge of our arrest. He was one of the persons involved in our arrest. When we were arrested under Milenko Karisik's command, he was involved in the arrest. That's why I am familiar with his name; although, everyone called him Mico. But I did not know his real name. All I knew was his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you knew that at the time, did you, before you were released from custody in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And later when I was held in detention, I heard that he had been relieved of his duties. So that's all I heard. And this is something that I heard in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you have any direct contact with that man - we know he's Mr. Davidovic - before your release from custody in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: No. I did not have any direct contact with him. I only had direct contact with Zeljko Lizdek and Dragan Andan, as I have said. I also had contacts on one occasion with Nikola Milanovic, who said that I should write a statement, that they would type it out, and that they should not beat me. They said that I was there to give a statement and that I shouldn't be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any complaints from anybody else who was in custody about Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: We weren't in the same place, so we couldn't speak about that. There were two of us in one cell; whereas, the others were in another cell. So we couldn't speak to each other to see whether anyone had complained about him, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I just remind you that you were eventually released. Did you at any time hear any complaint from anybody else who had been in custody in Bijeljina about Mr. Davidovic. Whether the complaint was during or after you were in custody, did you ever hear any complaint about Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 682
utterances.text: I didn't hear about anyone complaining about him directly, but I heard about people complaining about men under his command and they said that they'd been hit with baseball bats and they complained about how they had been arrested and treated, but I never saw anyone who said that he participated in such things. They would say that he issued orders and we would not even receive regular meals, and we really did not dare speak out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I was saying it hasn't been a long session. I notice the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in Courtroom II, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Courtroom II. And everyone is prepared to continue tomorrow in the afternoon at 3.00, courtroom still to be indicated. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
